opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it is that these frameworks, whether it's CrewAI or AutoGen or LangGraph, are really orchestration layers. They define how a set of agents talk to each other, hand off tasks, call tools, and iterate. What they need underneath is an inference platform that's fast and flexible, and that's where we come in.

From our perspective, there are a couple of key characteristics of agentic workloads that are quite different from the traditional chatbot setting. The first is that you're making many, many calls to models. An agent might plan, then reflect, then call a tool, then call another model to check the result. So the latency of each individual call compounds. If each step takes a few seconds, the whole workflow takes minutes, and that's not a good user experience. So tokens per second, and especially time to first token, really matter. That's something our reconfigurable dataflow architecture is very good at, because we can fuse the operations in a model and keep the data flowing on chip rather than bouncing back and forth to memory.

The second characteristic is that these workflows often don't use a single model. You might want a big reasoning model for planning, a smaller, faster model for routine steps, maybe a code-specialized model, maybe a domain-tuned model for a particular task. On GPU systems, switching between models is expensive, so people tend to provision separate hardware for each model, which is wasteful. Because of our three-tier memory system, with a large amount of DDR capacity alongside HBM and on-chip SRAM, we can hold many models resident on a single node and switch between them in milliseconds. That's what we've called composition of experts, and it maps really naturally onto agentic systems, where each agent can be backed by whichever model is most appropriate.

On the practical side, we expose all of this through OpenAI-compatible APIs, so developers using CrewAI or AutoGen don't have to change how they build. They just point their agents at our endpoints and pick the models they want. We've also put out examples and integrations so people can get started quickly.

So the short answer is: the frameworks handle the orchestration, and we focus on making the underlying inference fast, efficient, and able to serve lots of different models at once, because that's what makes agentic workflows actually practical in production.

r001.rationale: The response says agentic workflows may use multiple models and that the system can keep many resident and switch between them in milliseconds, connecting this capability to agentic systems built with orchestration frameworks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a lot, because the agentic workloads really change the profile of what you're asking the hardware to do. If you think about a traditional LLM serving scenario, you've got one model, you load it, you batch up requests, and you're optimizing throughput on that single model. With something like CrewAI or AutoGen, you've got multiple agents, often with different roles, and frequently you want different models behind those roles. You might want a big reasoning model for the planner, a smaller, faster model for tool calling or formatting, maybe a specialized model for code. And these agents are talking to each other in sequence, so latency per step compounds. If each hop is slow, the whole workflow is slow.

So the way we approach it on our system comes down to a couple of architectural properties. The first is the memory hierarchy. We have a very large amount of on-chip and near-chip memory relative to a GPU, and that lets us keep many models resident at once and switch between them in microseconds rather than milliseconds. On a GPU, if you want to swap from one model to another, you're typically reloading weights from HBM or even from host memory, and that kills you in a multi-agent setting. For us, the models are just sitting there, and the dataflow architecture lets us route a request to whichever model the agent needs essentially instantly. We call this composition of experts, and agentic frameworks are kind of the natural consumer of that capability.

The second piece is that these frameworks are very sensitive to time to first token and tokens per second on the decode side, because the agent loop is inherently sequential. The planner generates, the tool gets called, the result comes back, the next agent generates. You're not getting the benefit of big batches the way you do in offline inference. Our architecture is designed so that decode is fast even at low batch sizes, because we're not bound by moving weights back and forth from off-chip memory for every token. So you get this nice property where the single-stream speed is high, which is exactly what agent loops need.

And then from a software standpoint, we've tried to meet the frameworks where they are. We expose an OpenAI-compatible API, so if you've built your CrewAI or AutoGen application against that interface, you point it at our endpoint and it works. You don't have to rewrite anything. We also support the function calling and structured output pieces well, because that's where a lot of the agentic logic lives, and if the model can't reliably emit a tool call in the right format, the whole workflow breaks down regardless of how fast you are.

The thing I find exciting is that it changes what developers are willing to build. When each agent step is cheap and fast, you stop being so conservative about how many agents you use or how many iterations you let the loop run. You start to see workflows with dozens of model calls that still feel interactive to the user, and I think that's where the real value of agents shows up.

r001.rationale: The response says the system keeps many models resident and can switch between them in microseconds, then route each agent’s request to the model it needs in frameworks such as CrewAI or AutoGen.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that those frameworks are orchestrating a series of calls to models and tools. We want to make it easy for them to use our system for the model inference, without requiring developers to rewrite the orchestration layer.

And agentic workflows make inference performance particularly important. You’re no longer waiting for just one model response. An agent may make several calls, pass a result to another agent, and then use that result to decide what to do next. If those steps depend on one another, the latency accumulates. So the focus is on making the integration straightforward and making each model call fast enough that the overall workflow is useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes orchestrated model and tool calls and stresses fast inference, but it does not identify rapid switching among models as a supporting mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
The way we approach it is to support the models underneath those frameworks. So if you’re building an agentic workflow with CrewAI or AutoGen, you can use our system for the inference calls without having to rethink how you’ve organized your agents.

And performance becomes particularly interesting here because an agentic workflow can involve many sequential calls. One agent produces a result, another reasons about it, then perhaps you call a tool and come back to the model. The latency of those individual steps adds up. So making inference fast doesn’t just make an individual response faster; it makes these more complex workflows practical.

r001.rationale: The response says the system supports inference calls for workflows built with CrewAI or AutoGen and explains that faster inference helps sequential calls. It does not identify rapid switching among models as the support mechanism.
